newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Economic collapse leads to desperation in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Economic collapse leads to desperation in Kabul.

text.p: One Wednesday, Khowjan, an Afghan employee of a western aid agency, was supervising the distribution of aid to a crush of Kabul's poor from a school in 9-0pthe northwest of the city.

A huge crowd of women was waiting outside the gates of the school. Three hundred of them managed to push their way past the Taleban militia guards on the gate to force their way into the compound, said an eyewitness.

"It was muddy and many people, especially the children, were slipping and falling under the crowd. The aid workers were trying to pull up the children and organise the women," said the eyewitness who preferred to remain anonymous.
"Khowjan went down. No one saw exactly what happened. He managed to get up, but two or three hours later he fainted. He was taken to hospital, but he died."
The women were waiting for a distribution of stoves and charcoal, blankets, plastic sheeting and candles. Each allocation is worth less than $20.

The death of Khowjan is a painful illustration of the desperation of Kabul's citizens, particularly its women. For five years, since war engulfed the capital after the fall of the communists, the city has become progressively poorer and its inhabitants less able to afford the bare necessities of life.
The International Committee of the Red Cross recently completed a socio-economic survey in Kabul. They estimate that four out of five families in Kabul were in serious need.

"Generally speaking the socio-economic and food security situation could be described as serious for most families, with the exception of perhaps 20 per cent, for whom some assets were still owned and income available to ensure a satisfactory food supply for the family," said the survey report. According to ICRC relief delegate Patrick Vial, many Kabulis have already sold most of their belongings to survive.
"More and more people are becoming more and more vulnerable through decapitalisation. You go into their houses and you find that they have sold their blankets to buy food," said Vial.
The ICRC survey comes to some grim conclusions.

"Families are basically lacking the means to buy the food available in the markets because few members are able to find a job and obtain sufficient earnings, and because food prices keep increasing. As a result, they try to cope by selling assets, getting indebted, sending children out to collect wood or to work, and decreasing the quantities and variety of food consumed," said the survey.
Most families, it said, cannot afford to buy fuel to cook their food, and have to scavenge for it.
"About seven out of ten families use dead leaves, wooden cuts, and garbage collected outside as fuel for cooking food," it said.

The core of Kabul's problem is the collapse of the economy. What little industry the city once had has been destroyed by the factional fighting that followed the collapse of the communist regime in 1992.

The government was the last big employer in Kabul, but since the Taleban took over the city last September, few salaries have been paid. The situation has been exacerbated by the decline in value of the Afghani currency.
Most of the city's food is imported from Pakistan and the devaluation has had a direct effect on food prices.
"The economic situation is terrible. We are seeing more beggars and more children on the streets," said Ross Everson of the aid umbrella organisation Agency Co-ordinating Body for Afghan Relief.
Aid agencies are attempting to alleviate the situation. The United Nations World Food Programme estimated that almost half the city's one million inhabitants receive some kind of food aid.
Ismael Omar of WFP said the agency intends to increase its relief aid, particularly for women.
"We want to enlarge our women's projects. Most women, particularly widows, who have no other support are having problems," said Omar.
The ICRC is also in the process of expanding their assistance to women.

"Our surveys show that the most vulnerable group in Kabul consists of families headed by single women," said Vial. This has long been the case, he said, and has little to do with the Taleban's policy of denying women access to the workplace.
It was just these women whose desperation drove them to force the gate of the school in northwest Kabul, and ultimately led to the death of Khowjan.
